title: Frontend Security: XSS, CSRF, CSP & CORS
summary: The core frontend threats: **XSS** (injected script), **CSRF** (forged authenticated requests), and the defenses — **CSP**, safe output handling, `SameSite` cookies — plus **CORS**, the browser's cross-origin rules.

subtopics.title: XSS (Cross-Site Scripting)
subtopics.explanation: Attacker-controlled data is rendered as executable script. Defend by escaping/encoding output, avoiding innerHTML/dangerouslySetInnerHTML with untrusted data, and using a CSP.

subtopics.title: CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery)
subtopics.explanation: A malicious site triggers an authenticated request using the victim's cookies. Defend with SameSite cookies, CSRF tokens, and checking Origin.

subtopics.title: CSP (Content-Security-Policy)
subtopics.explanation: A response header that restricts which scripts/styles/origins can load, sharply limiting XSS impact.

subtopics.title: CORS
subtopics.explanation: The browser's rule that cross-origin responses are only readable if the server opts in with Access-Control-* headers. It protects users, not your server.

foundations.overview: Frontend security centers on a few threats. XSS is when untrusted data is injected and executed as script in your page — the most common frontend vulnerability. CSRF tricks a logged-in user's browser into making an authenticated request to your site. Defenses include escaping output, avoiding raw innerHTML with untrusted data, a Content-Security-Policy, SameSite cookies, and CSRF tokens. CORS is a related but separate browser mechanism controlling cross-origin reads.
foundations.formalDefinition: A set of browser-enforced threats and mitigations: XSS (script injection), CSRF (forged authenticated requests), CSP (script/source allowlisting), SameSite cookies, and CORS (cross-origin read policy).
foundations.whyItMatters: A single XSS hole can steal sessions and data for every user; these are the vulnerabilities that get frontends breached and are heavily probed in senior interviews.
foundations.mentalModel: Your page is a nightclub: XSS is a stranger sneaking in and acting as staff, CSRF is someone using a guest's coat-check ticket, CSP is the guest list, and CORS is the rule about who may read messages between clubs.
foundations.browserPerspective: The browser enforces the same-origin policy, CSP, and cookie rules; correct use of these is your primary defense surface.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Sanitizing user-generated content, setting a CSP, using httpOnly + SameSite cookies, adding CSRF protection to state-changing requests.
foundations.businessImpact: A breach is catastrophic to trust and often legally reportable; security work protects the whole business.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Security-aware components (no unsafe HTML injection, correct cookie flags) prevent whole classes of incidents.
foundations.performanceImpact: A strict CSP and avoiding heavy client-side sanitization libraries can also reduce risk without runtime cost.

commonMisconceptions.reality: CORS protects the user's browser from reading cross-origin responses; it is not server authorization — enforce that separately.
React escapes text by default, but dangerouslySetInnerHTML, injected URLs (javascript:), and unsanitized HTML still open XSS.

theory.question: How does XSS work and how do you defend against it?
theory.directAnswer: XSS happens when attacker-controlled data is rendered such that the browser executes it as script — for example inserting untrusted HTML via innerHTML, or a javascript: URL, or dangerouslySetInnerHTML. The attacker's script then runs with your page's privileges and can steal cookies/session or act as the user. Defenses: treat all user input as untrusted, escape/encode on output (frameworks like React escape text by default), never inject untrusted HTML without sanitizing, avoid unsafe sinks, set a Content-Security-Policy to restrict script sources, and keep session cookies httpOnly so script can't read them.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: The most common frontend vulnerability and its layered defenses.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: XSS is the #1 frontend security question and a real breach vector.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Untrusted data reaches an executable sink; escaping + CSP + safe sinks close it.

theory.whyImportant: One hole compromises every user, so defense-in-depth matters.

nestedTopics.title: Stored vs reflected XSS
nestedTopics.explanation: Stored persists in the DB and hits every viewer; reflected bounces off a URL/param for a targeted victim.

followUps.question: Where does CSP fit?
followUps.answer: It's defense-in-depth: even if an injection slips through, a strict CSP blocks the injected script from executing or exfiltrating.

keyTakeaways: XSS = injected script; escape output, avoid raw innerHTML, use a CSP.
CSRF = forged authenticated request; defend with SameSite cookies + tokens.
CSP allowlists sources and blunts XSS impact.
CORS controls cross-origin READS in the browser — it is not server auth.
Store auth in httpOnly + SameSite cookies, never plain localStorage for sensitive tokens.
